newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia to start talks with NATO despite expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia to start talks with NATO despite expansion.

text.p: Russia, in a key change of policy, said on Wednesday it would open talks with NATO on closer ties despite its unrelenting opposition to the alliance's plans to expand eastwards.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told his 16 NATO counterparts Moscow was ready to enter into a dialogue on a new relationship between the former Cold War foes which could take the form of a special charter or treaty.

"We were made an offer to hold consultations with NATO in order to settle any issues that might be of concern to us. We agreed to this offer. I think this will open the door to fruitful talks," Primakov later told reporters.

But a stern-faced Primakov quickly added Moscow had not dropped its all-out opposition to NATO's plans to take in new members from former communist central and Eastern Europe, set to be named at a Madrid summit of alliance leaders next July.
"This is based on the firm belief that it will inevitably lead to a new division of Europe. That is unacceptable," he said.

But apart from sounding a jarring -- albeit predictable -- note over enlargement, Primakov was in a relaxed, easy-going mood in keeping with the atmosphere which now reigns in regular encounters between the two old enemies.
The Russian stood before the press alongside a beaming NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana who repeated the alliance's wish to "build a solid partnership with Russia".
"We want to push this dialogue down the road... security in Europe cannot be established without Russia," he said.
The western allies, who want a new deal with Russia ready to be signed at their July 8-9 "enlargement summit", quickly hailed the Russian move as a breakthrough.
Previously, Moscow has demanded NATO put enlargement on ice before the start of any negotiations.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said he was "surprised and delighted by Russia's constructive attitude."
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who on Tuesday urged Moscow to "walk through the door" NATO had opened, described Primakov's agreement as "very good news".
"If a charter can be worked out between Russia and NATO, that will complete the integration of Europe, so we're started down the road of a unified, integrated Europe," he told reporters.
He said Russian fears over enlargement would prove groundless.
"There is no need to have enlargement re-divide Europe. On the contrary, enlargement can lead to the full integration of Europe," Christopher added.
Primakov said any NATO-Russia "document" should be far more than just a general set of principles and contain "very specific, very concrete" points addressing Moscow's security concerns.

NATO has authorised Solana to open talks, but member states have yet to agree his precise negotiating brief. NATO officials said this would be done very soon and they expected bargaining to begin in early January.

They said the expected negotiations would be hard with the Russians taking every opportunity to try and drive a wedge between the allies, many of whom are not sure how far they should go to satisfy Moscow's anxieties.

NATO foreign ministers, who on Tuesday set the date of the Madrid summit, later turned their attention to what to offer the countries wanting to join the alliance who are left out of the first wave of new members.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are the favourites to be invited to join out of a total of 11 countries now clamouring at NATO's door.
Christopher proposed the creation of a new Atlantic Partnership Council which would bring together some 27 of NATO's cooperation partners from central and eastern Europe under the same roof.
"It will give its members a formal consultative mechanism within the alliance and a mechanism for cooperating with each other," Christopher said.
The proposal was widely supported by other NATO members and the alliance's cooperation partners who held a joint ministerial session after the meeting with Primakov.
"The purpose of the summit is to bring all these countries -- Russia, partner countries, candidates for membership, everyone -- closer to NATO," said one senior official.
